# Hosted image maintenance

Image builds and boot tests use disposable GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners. Every published image must pass the guest SSH listener, HTTPS/DNS and reboot checks. Publication failure retains previous release assets.

CentOS Stream 8 is retired and its maintained guest validation failed after reboot in run [38635941548](https://github.com/oneclickvirt/pve_kvm_images/actions/runs/38635941548). Scheduled CentOS builds therefore select Stream 9 only. The `include_retired` manual input retains the repair path for Stream 8; it never bypasses boot validation or deletes existing images.

The published-image workflow accepts `acceleration=tcg` to force software emulation even when the hosted runner exposes KVM. This also forces the libguestfs overlay preparation and failure diagnostics to use TCG. Weekly smoke tests exercise both automatic acceleration and forced TCG; guest execution, SSH listener, verified HTTPS/DNS and a changed boot ID after reboot are required in both modes. The `maintained` scope covers the current maintained assets while `full` and exact filenames retain manual access to historical assets.

The published-image tests boot the released disk directly with QEMU. The separate weekly `Native PVE image smoke` workflow installs Proxmox from its signed official repository in a disposable Debian guest on a GitHub-hosted runner and reboots into the real PVE kernel. It restores four current Debian/Ubuntu templates through `pct`. When KVM is available for the PVE host, it also imports Debian 13 through `qm`, with KVM explicitly disabled for that inner VM. The cloud VM receives PVE-generated NoCloud network configuration, as real consumers provide. All image checks require guest execution, SSH listener, verified HTTPS/DNS and a changed boot ID after reboot.

Native checks verify release asset size and SHA256 before transferring inputs, never forward GitHub credentials into the PVE host or guests, and destroy the temporary host afterward. Provisioning, readiness and diagnostics have time limits; failed checks retain a failure conclusion and cannot change published images. Native progress streams to the runner log, with QGA output and serial diagnostics on failure. These current-version smoke results do not establish compatibility with every historical PVE release or image.

A software-emulated PVE host uses up to four available runner CPUs and 6 GiB of RAM when the runner has sufficient memory. In the default `vm_execution=auto` mode, a host without KVM still runs native `pct` checks, then stops before the VM is tested directly by QEMU on the runner, with TCG forced for both the guest and its libguestfs overlay. This avoids unreliable double software emulation. Each result names its backend (`pct`, `qm` or `qemu-tcg`); mixed results never emit the all-native success marker. An image failing its assertions still fails the workflow. Explicit `vm_execution=native` retains strict nested diagnostics and never falls back after a failure. Both PVE services must be active before native image testing. The overall job limit remains three hours.

Strict software-host diagnostics use PVE's VirtIO block disk attachment. Nested TCG with SCSI exposed the root partition only after initramfs had entered its emergency shell in [38846148430](https://github.com/oneclickvirt/pve_kvm_images/actions/runs/38846148430). With VirtIO block, [38856434856](https://github.com/oneclickvirt/pve_kvm_images/actions/runs/38856434856) mounted the root filesystem but then failed to exit initramfs, reporting a missing console and no init. The same released image passed direct TCG and native `qm` with a KVM outer host. Increasing the outer timeout cannot recover an emergency shell; these failures remain failures, and the default software-host path now avoids that double-emulation configuration. Native failure detection includes console/init errors and kernel panics. KVM-host tests continue to cover OVMF/q35/VirtIO SCSI. Manual runs may select VM-only scope to diagnose a failed VM without repeating container checks; the scope and input count are explicit in the log, and a VM-only run never establishes five-input coverage. These smoke checks cover five representative inputs, not every published image or every PVE version.
